Lloyds Banking Group stock: security chief appointment strengthens resilience
sum: Lloyds Banking Group appointed Manija Poulatova as Group Chief Security Officer on Friday, November 13, adding a senior leadership change to the bank's investor agenda. Poulatova takes up the role on Monday, November 16, according to the Lloyds Banking Group announcement.

Poulatova will report to Group Chief Operating Officer Ron van Kemenade and lead cyber security and technology resilience across Lloyds Banking Group's operations and brands. Her remit includes cyber governance and the protection of customer services as digital banking habits and technology continue to evolve.

She joined Lloyds in January 2024 and currently serves as Director of Security Engineering and Operations, where she leads more than 600 security specialists. Before joining Lloyds, she spent almost five years at Google Cloud and also worked at LogRhythm and Palo Alto Networks.

Poulatova succeeds Matt Rowe, who is leaving after more than four years as Chief Security Officer. Lloyds said Rowe strengthened cyber defences through greater automation, expanded proactive threat hunting and wider use of technologies including artificial intelligence.

The appointment comes as Lloyds continues to present security and technology as part of its broader transformation agenda. The group's investor page says Chief Financial Officer William Chalmers will join a JP Morgan UK Leaders Conference fireside chat on Tuesday, November 17, at 8:45 a.m.

sum: A 5.29% pre-market share price drop signaled investor unease at Lloyds Banking Group (LON: LLOY), even as the British lender posted robust nine-month financial results across the board.
The selloff reflected concern about what comes next, with management guiding toward a materially slower pace of net interest income growth heading into 2027.
Competitive pressure across mortgage, lending, and deposit markets is expected to constrain NII expansion to a mid-single-digit rate next year, trailing the stronger growth achieved through 2026.
Chief Executive Chalmers acknowledged that rivalry in both lending and deposit markets would partly erode the benefits the bank continues to derive from volume growth and structural hedge income.
The structural hedge, a key income driver, is forecast to generate more than £8 billion in 2027, but its annual growth contribution will shrink to roughly £1 billion from £1.5 billion the prior year.

That declining tailwind, combined with slower deposit market growth and the possibility of mortgage activity moderating if interest rates remain elevated, frames a more challenging revenue environment for the bank.
Despite the cautious forward guidance, Lloyds delivered strong underlying performance through the first nine months of 2026, with statutory profit after tax reaching £4.8 billion.

Analysts Have Just Cut Their Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (NSE:LLOYDSME) Revenue Estimates By 12%
sum: Today is shaping up negative for Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (NSE:LLOYDSME) shareholders, with the analysts delivering a substantial negative revision to this year's forecasts. This report focused on revenue estimates, and it looks as though the consensus view of the business has become substantially more conservative.

After this downgrade, Lloyds Metals and Energy's seven analysts are now forecasting revenues of ₹263b in 2027. This would be a meaningful 10% improvement in sales compared to the last 12 months. Statutory earnings per share are presumed to bounce 51% to ₹141. Before this latest update, the analysts had been forecasting revenues of ₹298b and earnings per share (EPS) of ₹141 in 2027. So there's been a clear change in analyst sentiment in the recent update, with the analysts making a substantial drop in revenues and reconfirming their earnings per share estimates.

The consensus has reconfirmed its price target of ₹2,133, showing that the analysts don't expect weaker sales expectationsthis year to have a material impact on Lloyds Metals and Energy's market value.

Taking a look at the bigger picture now, one of the ways we can understand these forecasts is to see how they compare to both past performance and industry growth estimates. We would highlight that Lloyds Metals and Energy's revenue growth is expected to slow, with the forecast 21% annualised growth rate until the end of 2027 being well below the historical 52% p.a. growth over the last five years. By way of comparison, the other companies in this industry with analyst coverage are forecast to grow their revenue at 11% annually. So it's pretty clear that, while Lloyds Metals and Energy's revenue growth is expected to slow, it's still expected to grow faster than the industry itself.

The most important thing to take away is that there's been no major change in sentiment, with analysts reconfirming that earnings per share are expected to continue performing in line with their prior expectations. Unfortunately, analysts also downgraded their revenue estimates, although our data indicates revenues are expected to perform better than the wider market. Often, one downgrade can set off a daisy-chain of cuts, especially if an industry is in decline.

Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited Earnings Missed Analyst Estimates: Here's What Analysts Are Forecasting Now
sum: Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (NSE:LLOYDSME) last week reported its latest second-quarter results, which makes it a good time for investors to dive in and see if the business is performing in line with expectations. It looks like a pretty bad result, all things considered. Although revenues of ₹57b were in line with analyst predictions, statutory earnings fell badly short, missing estimates by 31% to hit ₹18.38 per share. The analysts typically update their forecasts at each earnings report, and we can judge from their estimates whether their view of the company has changed or if there are any new concerns to be aware of. With this in mind, we've gathered the latest statutory forecasts to see what the analysts are expecting for next year.

Taking into account the latest results, the consensus forecast from Lloyds Metals and Energy's six analysts is for revenues of ₹298.2b in 2027. This reflects a major 24% improvement in revenue compared to the last 12 months. Statutory earnings per share are predicted to bounce 51% to ₹141. In the lead-up to this report, the analysts had been modelling revenues of ₹298.2b and earnings per share (EPS) of ₹141 in 2027. The consensus analysts don't seem to have seen anything in these results that would have changed their view on the business, given there's been no major change to their estimates.

With the analysts reconfirming their revenue and earnings forecasts, it's surprising to see that the price target rose 6.0% to ₹2,133. It looks as though they previously had some doubts over whether the business would live up to their expectations. Fixating on a single price target can be unwise though, since the consensus target is effectively the average of analyst price targets. As a result, some investors like to look at the range of estimates to see if there are any diverging opinions on the company's valuation. Currently, the most bullish analyst values Lloyds Metals and Energy at ₹2,389 per share, while the most bearish prices it at ₹1,879. This is a very narrow spread of estimates, implying either that Lloyds Metals and Energy is an easy company to value, or - more likely - the analysts are relying heavily on some key assumptions.

Lloyds shares at 94p! Time to sell?
sum: A fair few people got a fright in late October, including (probably) anyone taking a look at Lloyds' (LSE: LLOY) shares. The Halloween festivities coincided with the share price falling off a cliff on the back of a recent announcement by Chancellor John Healey of a windfall tax on banks. Lloyds' shares are now trading for pennies again – at 94p a pop, as I write.
Is a reversal of the 'banking surcharge' going to send shares in the Black Horse bank into a tailspin? Or is this simply market noise that's offering a chance to buy in cheap? Here's what I think.

Firstly, the much-predicted windfall tax was less impactful than it might have been. The basic detail is that the 'banking surcharge' has been temporarily increased for 15 months, taking it from 3% to 6%. The net effect is that banks like Lloyds will be losing 3% of earnings for just over a year.

A bigger impact in recent days was its 29 October earnings call. Shareholders might have been spooked by signs that things might be heading in the wrong direction. Net income increased 9% year on year, but there were worrying indications that margins are going to be squeezed. Net interest income's expected to be lower for 2027 on the back of competition in both lending and deposit markets. The share price dropped 6% on the day.

Eagle-eyed observers will however, note that the slide in Lloyds' shares – over 20%, meaning we are now firmly in crash territory – began all the way back in August. Not only that, but other FTSE 100 banks, and even ones abroad, are struggling too. So what the devil might be going on here?

One of the biggest issues for Lloyds is the short-term trajectory of the economy – in both the UK and the world at large. The success of banks is tied to the economies they operate in. More money flowing around means higher earnings.

So what's going on? Essentially, it's mostly down to the Iran war and its knock-on effects on inflation. Oil prices are loads higher than they were and shipping costs are on the up too. All this will have downstream effects on inflation.

sum: A Stocks and Shares ISA makes a brilliant home for dividend-paying UK shares. All shareholder payouts are tax-free, whether you reinvest them or draw them as income.

The good news is that plenty of FTSE 100 and FTSE 250 stocks offer attractive yields of 5%, 6% and in some cases more than 7%. With luck, that income should steadily rise as you reinvest dividends and companies increase payouts.
Nothing is guaranteed in investing, but I think these two FTSE 100 dividend stars are worth considering for an income portfolio today.
I’ve done brilliantly from wealth manager M&G (LSE: M&G). Its shares are up 20% over 12 months and 58% over five years, with dividends on top.

When I bought them, they yielded a stunning 10%. Such a dizzying yield can be a warning sign, but I believed it was sustainable. So far, I’ve been proved right. However, as the shares have climbed, the yield has slipped to 6.63% for new buyers. Still generous though. The board is also targeting annual dividend growth of around 2%. Although right now, that’s below inflation.
In the first half of 2026, M&G’s adjusted operating profit rose a solid 15% to £435m, driven by stronger asset-management revenues and growth in its life insurance business.

There are risks. A stock market crash could discourage customers from investing and reduce the commission-based fees M&G earns. It also operates in fiercely competitive markets, and is currently fighting a battle royale to win bulk annuity business from pension schemes. Passive tracker funds remain a constant challenge to its active management model.

The government needs the money to keep the fiscal headroom intact. That was a key manifesto promise. Another one of the promises made prior to the 2024 election was not to touch taxes on working people like income tax or VAT.

What will the impact be? This depends largely on the nature of any tax. A one-off raid is unlikely to make too much of a dent in the share price. A big and permanent levy on banking profits could do lasting damage to the sector.

The change in direction for interest rates has come as a shock to the markets. The expectation was a rate cut or three this year, down to perhaps 3%. Now that the Iran war has got inflation rearing its ugly head again, the current expectation is for one rate hike.

Higher interest rates is one reason for the success of banks in recent years because a bigger percentage means more room for a bigger margin. I’m talking about Hays (LSE:HAS). The recruitment company is down 53% over the past year, with 25% of that coming in just the past month.

The company’s core problem is that the hiring market has weakened sharply. Given that its revenue is tightly linked to hiring activity, this isn’t good. As a result, the half-year results released last month showed net fees fell by 9% versus the same period last year. Operating profit was down by 21% in what the CFO described as “a backdrop of continued macroeconomic and political uncertainty”.

Adding to the short-term woes was news that the CEO had suddenly stepped down, along with an 84% cut in the dividend. The dividend news obviously frightened away a lot of income investors. As for the CEO news, it’s not a good look for the future direction of the company if the key leader is changing unexpectedly.
The problems have pushed the stock down to 35p, the lowest level since the early 1990s.

To begin with, I noted down the current analyst ratings for the company. Of the 11 contributors I can see, the average target price for the coming year is 63p. The highest comes from Citibank, with a forecast of 90p. Interestingly, there are no target prices below 35p. This is a strong indication from experts that the recent fear about the stock is misplaced.

Another fundamental reason why I could consider buying is that the job market is cyclical. Over the decades, it has gone through good times and bad times. Right now is a bad time. But with a long-term investment view, I’m confident the market will improve in the coming years. As the UK economy recovers, with inflation hopefully continuing to fall and interest rates coming lower, it should act to kickstart economic growth. In turn, this should give employers more confidence to go out and hire.

“Reports that UK banks might get a reprieve in this week’s budget from previously floated new tax measures … underpinned the FTSE 100’s rise on Tuesday,” said Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell.

“It suggests that some intense lobbying by the industry has paid off, although U-turns have been a theme in UK politics for some time so banking boardrooms may not breathe a full sigh of relief until Rachel Reeves has sat down tomorrow afternoon.”

Speculation over potential bank tax rises has been swirling for months, having been revived in August when the IPPR thinktank argued that Reeves should levy a new bank tax to claw back money that commercial lenders earn from the Bank of England as result of an emergency economic policy known as quantitative easing put in place after the 2008 financial crisis.

The banking industry lobbied hard against a tax increase, arguing that banks in the UK were paying a total tax rate of about 45.8% when employment taxes and VAT were taken into account. That compared with a 38.6% rate in Frankfurt and 27.9% in New York.
